clue.text: Would a burst of speed be disastrous to it?

definitions.text: Would a burst of speed be disastrous to it?

parts.words: Would a burst of speed be disastrous to it?
parts.note: surface reading: a fragile vehicle that cannot take sudden acceleration
setter's reading: the small car is named after something that pops, so a burst would literally end it

explanation.surface: A worried motorist wonders whether flooring the accelerator will wreck a flimsy little car.
explanation.walkthrough: A BUBBLE CAR is a tiny 1950s-60s domed car such as the Isetta; bubbles burst, hence the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: The tiny domed microcar of the period took its name from its round glass canopy resembling a soap globe.

clue.text: The best a cook can do

definitions.text: The best a cook can do

parts.words: The best a cook can do
parts.note: surface reading: the finest result a cook can manage
setter's reading: a word that sounds a little like best and names a routine kitchen task

explanation.surface: Praise for a cook's finest effort.
explanation.walkthrough: To BASTE is to spoon fat or juices over roasting meat; the near-echo of 'best' carries the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Spooning melted fat over a joint while roasting is a basic cooking technique, something any cook does.

clue.text: Starting point of many a flight

definitions.text: Starting point of many a flight

parts.words: Starting point of many a flight
parts.note: surface reading: an airport or departure gate
setter's reading: the first flight of a fledgling leaving home

explanation.surface: A departure lounge from which many aeroplanes take off.
explanation.definitionFit: Young birds hatch and fledge in this structure, then make their first attempts at flying from its edge.

clue.text: It's not really a stone fruit

definitions.text: It's not really a stone fruit

parts.words: It's not really a stone fruit
parts.note: surface reading: a fruit such as a plum or cherry, built round a hard stone
setter's reading: a cross-bred fruit whose name contains a word for a small hard grain, though it is no true stone fruit

explanation.surface: A botanical quibble about whether some fruit counts as a drupe.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke rests on the word itself: LOGANBERRY ends in BERRY, and a berry is the textbook opposite of a stone fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A hybrid of raspberry and blackberry, it is a soft cane fruit rather than a drupe like a peach.

clue.text: More than one in succession

definitions.text: More than one in succession

parts.note: surface reading: several things happening one after another
setter's reading: succession as inheritance, with several people sharing it

explanation.surface: Several events following in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: People who jointly inherit an estate or title share the line of succession, so there is more than one heir.

clue.text: One girl gives the lie to another

definitions.text: another

parts.note: Rosa is a girl's name
taken as written

explanation.surface: One girl exposes another as a liar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gives the lie to' is an idiom for contradicting someone, but here it simply adds LIE to ROSA, producing a second girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The result is itself a girl's name, so it is literally another girl alongside the first one.

clue.text: A revolutionary sort of 22

definitions.text: A revolutionary
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a part that spins round

definitions.text: sort of 22
definitions.meaning: second meaning: 22-across is a word reading the same both ways, and this is one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' suggests a rebel, but it means something that turns. ROTOR reads the same backwards, an example of 22-across.
explanation.definitionFit: The spinning part of a helicopter or engine turns round, and its letters are symmetrical front to back.

clue.text: Presumably not a suitable resort for Nonconformists

definitions.text: Presumably not a suitable resort for Nonconformists

parts.words: Presumably not a suitable resort for Nonconformists
parts.note: surface reading: a holiday town that would not appeal to rebels
setter's reading: Protestant dissenters, who would hardly go to the seat of the Pope

explanation.surface: A travel note warning rebels off a particular holiday spot.
explanation.walkthrough: Nonconformists are English Protestants outside the Church of England, such as Methodists and Baptists; Rome is the centre of Catholicism.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian capital houses the Vatican, home of the Catholic Church, which Protestant dissenters reject.

clue.text: He doesn't pass false notes

definitions.text: He doesn't pass false notes

parts.note: surface reading: an honest person who won't spend forged banknotes
setter's reading: musical notes out of pitch, which a piano specialist corrects

explanation.surface: An honest man refuses to circulate counterfeit money.
explanation.definitionFit: A piano technician adjusts strings until each pitch is true, letting no off-key sound go uncorrected.

clue.text: Prince of athletes?

definitions.text: Prince of athletes?

parts.note: surface reading: the greatest sportsman
setter's reading: a prince is royal, and an athlete representing Oxford or Cambridge is a Blue

explanation.surface: Hailing a champion as the prince among sportsmen.
explanation.walkthrough: A Blue is an Oxford or Cambridge sportsman who has represented the university; a prince is royal, so a royal Blue.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a deep bright shade of the colour, traditionally associated with the British monarchy.

clue.text: Youngster gives physical research society one thousand dollars

definitions.text: Youngster

parts.note: the Society for Psychical Research; 'physical' is probably a misprint for psychical
the Roman numeral for one
G, a grand, is slang for a thousand dollars

explanation.surface: A young person donates a thousand dollars to a scientific society.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprig, literally a small shoot, is a dated word for a young person, especially a lively youth.

clue.text: Not ' the kind that talks, evidently

definitions.text: Not ' the kind that talks, evidently

parts.words: Not ' the kind that talks, evidently
parts.note: surface reading: someone quiet, not a chatterbox
setter's reading: the saying that money talks, and a payment made to buy silence

explanation.surface: A remark about a person who keeps quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'money talks' means wealth carries influence; a bribe paid for silence is the exception.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a bribe paid to keep someone silent about a secret, so it buys quiet rather than speaking.

clue.text: Without them one can do nothing

definitions.text: Without them one can do nothing

parts.words: Without them one can do nothing
parts.note: surface reading: some helpers or tools a person is helpless without
setter's reading: things so basic that nothing is possible lacking them

explanation.surface: A complaint that someone is helpless without certain people.
explanation.definitionFit: Indispensable basics are by definition the things that cannot be done without, the absolute necessities.

clue.text: A matter of morals when in manuscript

definitions.text: A matter
definitions.note: oral as a noun, a spoken examination

indicators.note: manuscript is abbreviated MS, and the wanted word sits inside those two letters, so we take what lies between them

parts.note: the word without its outer M and S

explanation.surface: An ethical issue raised by a manuscript.
explanation.walkthrough: MS is the standard abbreviation for manuscript; ORAL placed inside M...S spells MORALS.
explanation.definitionFit: A spoken examination, such as a viva, is called an oral, a matter dealt with by speech not writing.

clue.text: It's the Mods who might go to church

definitions.text: who might go to church

parts.note: every letter of the phrase is used

explanation.surface: A surprised remark that the scooter-riding Mods are the churchgoers.
explanation.walkthrough: Mods were 1960s British youth on scooters, not obvious churchgoers. There is no anagram signal; old clues often left it out.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the Protestant denomination founded by John Wesley attend chapel services, so they are people who go to worship.

clue.text: They enable one to keep in touch

definitions.text: They enable one to keep in touch

parts.words: They enable one to keep in touch
parts.note: surface reading: letters or telephones that keep people in contact
setter's reading: the literal sense of touch, as with an insect's antennae

explanation.surface: Something that helps friends stay in contact.
explanation.definitionFit: Antennae of insects and similar organs are sensory projections used to sense surroundings by contact.

clue.text: A charlady, perhaps?

definitions.text: A charlady, perhaps?

parts.note: surface reading: a cleaning woman
setter's reading: char is also a kind of fish, so a char lady sells it

explanation.surface: A guess that someone is a cleaning woman.
explanation.walkthrough: A charlady is a British cleaning woman; char is also a freshwater fish related to trout.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who sells seafood at a market might well deal in char, the trout-like freshwater species.

clue.text: Are lent for all time

definitions.text: for all time

parts.note: every letter of the two words is used

explanation.surface: Some things are loaned out permanently.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no anagram signal word; older clues sometimes omitted one.
explanation.definitionFit: Something everlasting lasts forever, without beginning or end, which is lasting through every age.

clue.text: Put to sleep in a draughty way?

definitions.text: Put to sleep in a draughty way?

parts.words: Put to sleep in a draughty way?
parts.note: surface reading: dozing off in a chilly breezy room
setter's reading: by means of a draught, a dose of sleeping medicine

explanation.surface: Someone nodding off in a room full of cold air.
explanation.walkthrough: A sleeping draught is a drink of medicine that brings sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: To drug someone into unconsciousness with an opiate or sedative is to send them to sleep chemically.

clue.text: Does it describe the seamy side of surgery?

definitions.text: Does it describe the seamy side of surgery?

parts.words: Does it describe the seamy side of surgery?
parts.note: surface reading: the sordid underside of the medical world
setter's reading: seamy taken literally, to do with stitched seams

explanation.surface: A question about the scandalous side of operating theatres.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective relates to stitches closing a wound, the seams a surgeon sews after operating.

clue.text: A man of drive with a good display of plate

definitions.text: A man of drive with a good display of plate

parts.words: A man of drive with a good display of plate
parts.note: surface reading: an ambitious man showing off his silverware
setter's reading: drive as in driving a car, and plate as the L-plate a novice must show

explanation.surface: An energetic go-getter who shows off his silver.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain and Australia a novice driver must display an L-plate, a red L on white, front and back.
explanation.definitionFit: A trainee motorist who has not passed the test must display the letter L on the car.

clue.text: Yggdrasil — before or after burning?

definitions.text: Yggdrasil — before or after burning?

parts.note: surface reading: the world tree of Norse myth
setter's reading: the species of the world tree is also what is left after any wood is burnt

explanation.surface: A riddle about the mythical Norse world tree going up in flames.
explanation.walkthrough: Yggdrasil is an ASH TREE in Norse myth; after burning, a tree becomes ash, so the name fits either way.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norse world tree is described in the Eddas as a giant specimen of the genus Fraxinus.

clue.text: They can't help being beastly to one another

definitions.text: They can't help being beastly to one another

parts.words: They can't help being beastly to one another
parts.note: surface reading: people who are always nasty to each other
setter's reading: beastly taken literally, as being beasts in each other's eyes

explanation.surface: A couple who cannot stop being horrid to each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Creatures of the animal kingdom are literally beasts, so each appears as a beast to the other.

clue.text: Whereby he gave his wife a bed

definitions.text: Whereby he gave his wife a bed

parts.words: Whereby he gave his wife a bed
parts.note: surface reading: some means by which a man presented his wife with a bed
setter's reading: Shakespeare, who famously left his wife his second-best bed in his testament

explanation.surface: How a husband came to give his wife a bed.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's will left Anne Hathaway 'my second best bed', a famous bequest; the name WILL is a bonus nod to him.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal document disposing of property at death is how a bequest such as a bed is passed on.

clue.text: Where all is forgotten but a bare leg?

definitions.text: Where all is forgotten

parts.note: a leg is a limb
bare, with nothing on it: O is nothing

explanation.surface: A place of oblivion, or perhaps just someone's bare leg.
explanation.walkthrough: A leg with nothing on it is LIMB plus O; there may also be a nod to the limbo dance, done with bare legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Limbo is a state of oblivion or neglect, the place where forgotten things are consigned, from the theological border region of hell.

clue.text: Put in a word for Mum, and Dad, too

definitions.text: Put in a word for Mum, and Dad, too

parts.words: Put in a word for Mum, and Dad, too
parts.note: surface reading: speaking up on behalf of both parents

parts.words: a word for Mum, and Dad
parts.note: setter's reading: a term that describes both those words, which read the same backwards

explanation.surface: A child pleads on behalf of both parents.
explanation.walkthrough: MUM and DAD each read the same either way, so they are both PALINDROMEs.
explanation.definitionFit: A term for any word or phrase spelt identically forwards and backwards, as both parent names are.

clue.text: Those showing characteristic spirit

definitions.text: characteristic spirit

parts.note: every letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: Some people display a typical spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no anagram signal word, a common laxity in older puzzles.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the distinctive character, values and attitudes of a community or group.

clue.text: Language of the — upper set

definitions.text: Language

indicators.note: of here means taken out of, so the wanted letters come from within the words that follow

parts.note: found across the two words

explanation.surface: The way the upper class speaks.
explanation.walkthrough: Erse is an old name for the Gaelic of Ireland or Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Erse is a dated term for the Gaelic tongue, a Celtic speech of Ireland and the Scottish Highlands.

clue.text: Notes made by a modern Ma

definitions.text: Notes

indicators.note: made means constructed or fashioned, so the following letters are built into a new order

parts.note: every letter of the phrase is used

explanation.surface: A contemporary mother writes reminders.
explanation.definitionFit: Memoranda are written reminders or brief official messages, the plural of memorandum.

clue.text: His muscles "are strong as iron bands"

definitions.text: His muscles "are strong as iron bands"

parts.note: surface reading: some strongman's physique
setter's reading: a line from a Longfellow poem about a village craftsman at his forge

explanation.surface: Admiring a strongman whose muscles are like iron.
explanation.walkthrough: Longfellow wrote of the village SMITH: 'the muscles of his brawny arms are strong as iron bands'.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's hero is a blacksmith, a metalworker who hammers iron at the forge, here shortened.

clue.text: To whom Hamlet compared his mourning mother

definitions.text: To whom Hamlet compared his mourning mother

parts.words: To whom Hamlet compared his mourning mother
parts.note: surface reading: a question about Shakespeare's play
setter's reading: in his first soliloquy Hamlet likens his mother at the funeral to a weeping figure of Greek myth

explanation.surface: A literature question about Hamlet and his grieving mother.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth NIOBE wept endlessly for her slain children and was turned to stone.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet's first soliloquy likens Gertrude at the funeral to the weeping mythological mother of slain children.

clue.text: Not suitable members of a Co-operative Society

definitions.text: Not suitable members of a Co-operative Society

parts.words: Not suitable members of a Co-operative Society
parts.note: surface reading: people who would not fit in a co-op shop's membership
setter's reading: co-operative as willing to go along, the opposite of people who fight back

explanation.surface: Undesirable recruits for a co-op store's membership.
explanation.walkthrough: The Co-operative Society is a British member-owned retail chain; those who oppose would hardly co-operate.
explanation.definitionFit: People who oppose or fight back are the opposite of co-operative, so they would hardly belong.
